Hospitals and senior living. Heat is never cut. Pays a small guarantee premium.
Year-round hot-water users. Heat all year, so summer heat is used, not wasted.
Space-heating users. Cheapest heat; curtailed first when supply is short (boiler takes over).

rules.rule: Export is a second sink, never the only one
rules.how: The data center keeps its own heat-rejection plant (air-cooled dry coolers, as designed) sized for 100% of its heat, with its own redundancy. HeatOS adds a free extra place for the heat to go. Nothing about its cooling design depends on us.

A fail-open valve sits between the data center's loop and the network. If the network trips, loses flow or runs hot, the valve sends all the water back through the data center's own coolers within about 30 seconds. The data center's temperature setpoint is never changed by us.

rules.rule: Never export more than 80% of the heat
rules.how: Its own coolers always carry a base load and stay warm and tested. In this plan the peak hour exports 2.6% of the heat, so the rule is met.
A plate heat exchanger keeps the data center's coolant apart from the network water, so a pipe leak outside cannot reach the computers.

Customers take heat out, so the water that comes back is cooler than what went out. That is free pre-cooling for the data center and the reason the plan frees cooling electricity (see the data-center benefits).

match_scorecard.headline: All of the heat is used directly: no heat pump needed
match_scorecard.how: The data center's water is at about 50 C. Low-temperature users (greenhouses, radiant floors, new buildings, mild-weather radiators) take it directly. Hot water (60 C) and cold-weather radiators get a heat pump that lifts only the difference, so the less lift, the less electricity.

match_scorecard.headline: Peak export 2.3 MW against 72.0 MW available (3.2%)
match_scorecard.how: Checked for every hour of 12 typical days: the heat customers can draw never exceeds what the data center can give. Each heat pump covers only part of its building's coldest hour; the boiler covers the rest.

match_scorecard.headline: Winter export is 92% flat across the day (average / peak)
match_scorecard.how: Computers make heat all day. Homes peak morning and evening, offices by day, hotels and hot-water users run through the night. Mixing them flattens the draw so it matches a flat supply; the tiers decide who goes first if it ever does not.

match_scorecard.headline: 3% of the data center's heat is used in winter, 1% in summer; 55% of delivered heat is year-round load
match_scorecard.how: Heating demand follows the weather; hot water and process heat (such as a greenhouse) do not. Customers are chosen with their summer baseload in mind, so the summer heat is used rather than wasted.

match_scorecard.headline: 99.91% expected network availability; every customer keeps its boiler
match_scorecard.how: Expected time off the network comes from failure rates (data center trip, a break on the customer's own pipe path, building equipment). Storage rides through short trips, valves isolate a broken branch, and the customer's boiler starts by itself within about 10 minutes. Protected and firm customers are the last to be cut when supply is short.

architecture_why: The source is already hot (about 50 C) because the computers are liquid-cooled, so greenhouses and fish tanks can use the heat directly with no heat pump.
Customers are spread out, so the network is short and goes first to the large year-round users next to the campus; homes and schools follow only if the heat per metre of pipe justifies it.
A pit or tank store on open land is cheap and rides through short outages; the campus design is closed-loop with dry cooling, so no water is added and nothing is discharged to Cayuga Lake.
Return water at about 30 C is the cascade: the hottest users take heat first, then lower-temperature users, and the coolest water goes back to the data center.
Pipes follow existing roads and avoid wetlands; pumps and controls stay above grade pending the flood review.

regenerative_scorecard.headline: 2,752 t CO2 avoided per year by displacing gas, propane and oil
regenerative_scorecard.site_says: The grid here is largely zero-carbon, the data center is all-electric with no stack emissions, and many homes still burn propane and heating oil.
regenerative_scorecard.plan_does: Moves heating from fossil fuel to captured server heat. Because the electricity is clean, each unit of heat moved saves a lot of carbon.

regenerative_scorecard.headline: 3.0 t NOx and 165 kg PM2.5 avoided per year
regenerative_scorecard.site_says: Air is already very clean (ozone 20th percentile, PM2.5 4th percentile, no days worse than 'Good').
regenerative_scorecard.plan_does: The air-quality gain is small because the starting point is already good, so the case for Lansing rests on cost, carbon and local ownership more than on air.

regenerative_scorecard.headline: Closed loop, almost no extra water, nothing new to Cayuga Lake
regenerative_scorecard.site_says: Cayuga Lake is impaired with phosphorus and storm runoff reaches it. The data center is designed as a closed loop with dry cooling and uses water only on about 10 to 20 peak days a year.
regenerative_scorecard.plan_does: Heat export carries warm water to customers and brings it back cooler in sealed pipes: no discharge to the lake and no new intake. Water saved is small because little is used.

regenerative_scorecard.headline: Heating demand -8% by 2050; year-round share of delivered heat 58%
regenerative_scorecard.site_says: About 3 F warmer by 2050 and 3 more inches of rain within 10 years. Flood maps for the site need a closer look.
regenerative_scorecard.plan_does: Greenhouse and fish-farm customers need heat in every month, so they hold their value as winters warm. Pumps and controls stay above grade until the flood review is done.

regenerative_scorecard.headline: 2 new local businesses supplied; heat priced 20% below today
regenerative_scorecard.site_says: Poverty and minority populations are low locally (28th and 24th percentiles), but homes on propane and oil carry the highest heating costs.
regenerative_scorecard.plan_does: Homes are not connected yet because the pipe per home costs too much. Priority goes to low-income and manufactured-home neighborhoods, and the 'next in line' list shows the grant each group would need to join.

regenerative_scorecard.headline: New year-round farm jobs next to the plant; no change to the data center's footprint
regenerative_scorecard.site_says: The site is a former coal plant on an industrial parcel away from homes, and the developer plans an annual fund for schools, parks and community initiatives.
regenerative_scorecard.plan_does: Cheap heat is what makes a greenhouse and a fish farm possible here, and local ownership keeps the heat income in the community.

Needs heat in every month (55% of its heat is year-round load), so the data center's summer heat is used, not wasted.
All of its heat needs no heat pump: the water is already hot enough.
